summary:
## Producer Price Nine-Month Rally

May's producer price index climbed 0.8% month-over-month to reach 129.82, extending its ninth consecutive month of gains. Year-over-year, the index surged 8.5% compared to May last year, marking the steepest increase in three years and ten months since the Ukraine war spike of July 2022 at 9.2%. This represents the second-longest consecutive rise on record, following a thirteen-month streak from November 2020. The persistent upward pressure reflects ongoing global supply chain disruptions and energy market volatility stemming from Middle Eastern geopolitical tensions.

## Chemical Products Fuel Inflation Spread

While oil and coal prices showed modest declines last month, the inflation burden has broadened to encompass chemical products, financial service charges, and city gas. Financial transaction fees surged 22.0%, driven by robust stock market performance, while industrial city gas prices jumped over 10.0% due to lingering concerns about energy supply following Middle Eastern instability. Solvent prices, used primarily for dry cleaning, skyrocketed 239.6%, while sulfuric acid climbed 215.9%. This diversification of inflationary pressures suggests the cost-push effects are entrenching across multiple sectors rather than concentrating solely in energy commodities.

## Grain Prices Extend Four-Month Climb

Commodity prices, particularly grains and livestock feed, continue rising and are expected to ripple through processed food prices in the second half. The combination of elevated agricultural input costs and the ongoing Ukraine conflict ramifications—which analysts suggest will impact markets for three months to one year—poses downside risks to inflation expectations. Korea's central bank acknowledged that while May's monthly increase of 0.8% represented a slowdown from prior months, the narrowing of oil's contribution signals inflation is becoming harder to control through commodity price reversals alone.

## Seoul Real Estate Transitions From Rentals to Sales

The '2030 dream' homebuying surge has dramatically shifted Seoul's property landscape. Middle and outer-ring districts including Jungnang and Nowon saw listings plummet 12.0% and 8.0% respectively as prospective buyers migrate from impossible jeonse rental situations toward ownership. The Sagajeong Central I-Park complex in Jungnang's Myeongmok-dong recorded new high prices, with an 84-square-meter unit selling for 1.52 billion won on May 13th. First-half projections indicate nationwide jeonse prices will rise 3.6% through year-end, substantially outpacing the anticipated 1.5% appreciation in sales prices as supply constraints from construction delays and redevelopment project stalls compound housing shortages.

## Small Business Debt Relief and Regional Guarantee Expansion

The government announced comprehensive small-business support measures, allocating 2.2 trillion won to resolve non-performing loans while establishing 2.0 trillion won in new regional specialty guarantees. This restructuring of the regional credit guarantee system aims to stabilize job creation for youth and address liquidity pressures facing small enterprises. Concurrent regulatory improvements include consolidated subscription service management and streamlined maritime infrastructure development, signaling coordinated efforts to sustain economic activity across multiple sectors during the producer price inflation cycle.

## KOSPI Breaches 9,300 as Market Capitalization Hits 8 Quadrillion Won

South Korea's benchmark KOSPI index pierced the historic 9,300-point level, driven predominantly by semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. National market capitalization surpassed 8,137 trillion won for the first time, with the main KOSPI board reaching 7,591 trillion won and KOSDAQ contributing 546 trillion won. SK Hynix alone achieved market capitalization exceeding 2,000 trillion won, positioning it second only to Samsung Electronics. Despite the euphoric index performance, underlying market breadth reveals concerning divergence—only 11.0% of KOSPI constituents advanced alongside the index gains, with growing performance gaps between semiconductor leaders and mid-cap diversified stocks.

## Dollar-Won Exchange Rate Remains Elevated Despite Iran Peace Agreement

The won-dollar exchange rate hovered around 1,537 won per dollar, appreciating only minimally despite the preliminary ceasefire agreement between the United States and Iran. The extended high exchange rate environment reflects lingering risk premiums as markets digest whether the Hormuz Strait reopening will durably reduce geopolitical risk. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Walsh's inaugural FOMC meeting maintained accommodative policy while signaling the committee's commitment to price stability, but market participants anticipate continued rate increases through 2026, supporting sustained dollar strength against emerging market currencies.

## New Nuclear Plants Selected for Construction at Yeongdeok and Gijang

The Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power Company announced site selections for new reactors: two large-capacity units in North Gyeongbuk's Yeongdeok and one small modular reactor in Busan's Gijang. This marks the first new nuclear facility designation in fifteen years, responding to surging electricity demand driven by artificial intelligence deployment and electric vehicle proliferation. The dual-track energy strategy reflects government commitment to both renewable energy expansion and stable baseload generation through nuclear sources, addressing concerns about grid reliability amid rapid electrification.

## Implications for Investors and Households

Investors face a complex landscape requiring careful sector selection. While semiconductor leadership continues driving indices higher, broader market participation suggests rotational risks warrant diversification beyond mega-cap technology stocks. The persistent producer price inflation cycle—now in its ninth consecutive month—threatens margin compression for manufacturing and consumer-focused companies unless wage pressures remain contained. Real estate participants should monitor jeonse-to-sales transitions closely, as the 3.6% anticipated jeonse appreciation may eventually compress rental yields and accelerate further price normalization.

For household consumers, the extended producer price inflation period indicates sustained pricing pressure on groceries, utilities, and services extending into the second half. The government's 2.2 trillion won small-business debt relief may provide temporary relief, but underlying cost pressures persist. The won's exchange rate stability near 1,537 won per dollar will support import costs, though semiconductor and manufacturing export competitiveness could benefit from further appreciation if geopolitical stability confirms.
headline: Producer Price Inflation Persists as Markets Surge on Middle East Peace Deal
